transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. What brings you to see me today?

Well... I suppose I'm just here because I've been feeling, I don't know, wound up. Like I'm just constantly running on a motor lately. I finish one thing, whether it's at school or at home, and... I just immediately jump to the next thing. It's like I can't shut myself off.
Have you noticed a decreased need for sleep, feeling rested after only a few hours?
No. I... I still need to sleep. I definitely don't feel rested if I only get a few hours.
Do you find yourself constantly worrying about a lot of different everyday things, and having a hard time controlling those worries?
No, I... I wouldn't say that. I don't really spend a lot of time worrying about things.
Do you often have trouble keeping your focus on tasks or schoolwork?
No, not really. I... I can focus fine. Getting through my work isn't the issue.
Do you often find yourself fidgeting with your hands or feet, or squirming when you have to stay seated?

Yeah, I guess so. Um... like in IEP meetings, or... my admin classes. I don't really notice I'm doing it at first. But my leg will be bouncing under the table, or I'm clicking a pen... shifting around in the chair a lot. I usually only realize it when people start glancing over at me.
Did you experience this kind of restlessness or being constantly on the go when you were a child, before the age of 12?

Yeah... I suppose so. It's not really a new thing. 

Um... my mother used to joke about it. She'd say that even back in elementary school, I was trying to teach the class from my seat. I guess I was just always getting out of my chair... talking, or cutting in before the teacher even finished giving directions. 

So, yeah. It's been part of who I am for a long time. It isn't just something that started up recently with this... family change.

inference_history.note: Initial differential based on patient reporting feeling constantly wound up, driven as if by a motor, and unable to turn off: consider hypomanic/manic episode (Bipolar disorder), generalized anxiety disorder, and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder.
